source.text: וַיְהִ֤י הָעָם֙ כְּמִתְאֹ֣נְנִ֔ים רַ֖ע בְּאָזְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וַיִּשְׁמַ֤ע יְהוָה֙ וַיִּ֣חַר אַפּ֔וֹ וַתִּבְעַר־בָּם֙ אֵ֣שׁ יְהוָ֔ה וַתֹּ֖אכַל בִּקְצֵ֥ה הַֽמַּחֲנֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And were the people like complainers [of] evil in [the] ears of Yahweh; and heard Yahweh, and burned his anger, and burned among them [the] fire of Yahweh, and consumed in [the] edge of the camp.

en.L: And the people were like those complaining [of] evil in the ears of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} heard, and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger burned, and the fire of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} burned among them and consumed [some] in the edge of the camp.
en.B: Now the people began complaining about their hardships in the hearing of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. When {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} heard it, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger flared up, and fire from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} broke out among them and burned up part of the outer edge of the camp.
en.R: The people started to complain about how hard things were, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} heard them. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} became very angry. Fire from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} began to burn among them, and it burned up some of the edge of the camp.

decisions.choice: like complainers of evil: the people fell into grumbling about their troubles
decisions.reason: The verb for complaining is rare (elsewhere only Lamentations 3:39). "Like" can mean the people behaved as complainers, or that what they said sounded like complaint in God's hearing. "Evil" here is the hardship they complained about: the journey had just begun again (10:33), and the text does not say what troubled them.

decisions.choice: the fire of Yahweh: fire sent by Yahweh as judgment
decisions.reason: The same phrase names the fire that came from Yahweh and consumed Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:2) and the 250 men who offered incense (Numbers 16:35). Here it reaches only the edge of the camp, a warning more than a destruction.

decisions.choice: consumed [some] in the edge of the camp
decisions.reason: The verb has no object; the preposition "in" means the fire ate into part of the edge of the camp. Literal brackets "some"; Balanced and Readable say "part of" and "some of".

source.text: וַיִּצְעַ֥ק הָעָ֖ם אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֑ה וַיִּתְפַּלֵּ֤ל מֹשֶׁה֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֔ה וַתִּשְׁקַ֖ע הָאֵֽשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: And cried out the people to Moses, and prayed Moses to Yahweh, and sank the fire.

en.L: And the people cried out to Moses, and Moses prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and the fire sank down.
en.B: The people cried out to Moses, and Moses prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and the fire died down.
en.R: The people cried out to Moses for help. Moses prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and the fire went out.

decisions.choice: Moses prays and the fire dies down: Moses stands between the people and God
decisions.reason: The people do not pray themselves; they cry out to Moses, and he prays for them. Moses does the same again in 12:13, 14:13-19 and 21:7.

decisions.choice: cried out to Moses for help
decisions.reason: The verb means a cry of distress. Readable adds "for help" to show what kind of cry it was.

source.text: וַיִּקְרָ֛א שֵֽׁם־הַמָּק֥וֹם הַה֖וּא תַּבְעֵרָ֑ה כִּֽי־בָעֲרָ֥ה בָ֖ם אֵ֥שׁ יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And called [one] [the] name of the place the that Taberah, because burned among them [the] fire of Yahweh.

en.L: And [one] called the name of that place Taberah, because the fire of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} burned among them.
en.B: So that place was named Taberah, because the fire of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had burned among them.
en.R: So that place was called Taberah, which means "burning." It got that name because fire from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had burned among them there.

decisions.choice: Taberah: "burning", a name taken from what happened there
decisions.reason: The place name comes from the same root as the verb "burned" in this verse and in verse 1. The place appears again in the list of Israel's offenses in Deuteronomy 9:22. It is not in the list of camps in Numbers 33, so it may be a spot near the camp at Kibroth-hattaavah (verse 34) rather than a separate stop.

decisions.choice: called: someone named it; the subject is left unstated
decisions.reason: The verb is singular with no subject, the Hebrew way of saying "it was named". It may mean Moses or the people in general.

decisions.choice: which means "burning"
decisions.reason: Readable explains the name, since the story turns on its meaning.

source.text: וְהָֽאסַפְסֻף֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּקִרְבּ֔וֹ הִתְאַוּ֖וּ תַּאֲוָ֑ה וַיָּשֻׁ֣בוּ וַיִּבְכּ֗וּ גַּ֚ם בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ מִ֥י יַאֲכִלֵ֖נוּ בָּשָֽׂר׃

records.literal_gloss: And the rabble that [was] in its midst craved a craving, and returned and wept also [the] sons of Israel, and said, who will feed us meat?

en.L: And the rabble that [was] among them craved a craving, and the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel also wept again, and said, "Who will feed us meat?
en.B: The mixed crowd among them was seized by craving, and the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} began to weep again too. They said, "If only we had meat to eat!
en.R: The outsiders who were traveling with the people began to long for better food. Then the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} started crying again too. They said, "We wish we had meat to eat!

decisions.choice: the rabble: a gathered mob, probably the non-Israelites who left Egypt with Israel
decisions.reason: The word appears only here. It comes from a verb meaning "gather" and suggests a collection of people, a crowd brought together from anywhere. The verse sets them apart from "the sons of Israel also", so they are most likely the "mixed crowd" that went up from Egypt with Israel (Exodus 12:38).

decisions.choice: craved a craving: a strong, consuming desire
decisions.reason: The verb and its noun from the same root stress the strength of the desire. The same word gives the place its name in verse 34, "graves of craving".

decisions.choice: who will feed us meat?: a wish, not a real question
decisions.reason: "Who will ...?" is a Hebrew way of saying "if only someone would ..." (as in 2 Samuel 23:15). The people are not asking who will provide meat; they are complaining that they have none.

decisions.choice: returned and wept: wept again
decisions.reason: "Returned" before another verb means the act happened again. Israel had complained about food before, in the wilderness of Sin (Exodus 16:2-3), where God gave both quail and manna.

decisions.choice: the mixed crowd (Balanced); the outsiders who were traveling with the people (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the phrase that links this group to Exodus 12:38; Readable says plainly who they probably were. Literal keeps "rabble", the sense of the word itself.

source.text: זָכַ֨רְנוּ֙ אֶת־הַדָּגָ֔ה אֲשֶׁר־נֹאכַ֥ל בְּמִצְרַ֖יִם חִנָּ֑ם אֵ֣ת הַקִּשֻּׁאִ֗ים וְאֵת֙ הָֽאֲבַטִּחִ֔ים וְאֶת־הֶחָצִ֥יר וְאֶת־הַבְּצָלִ֖ים וְאֶת־הַשּׁוּמִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: We remember the fish which we ate in Egypt for nothing, the cucumbers and the melons and the leeks and the onions and the garlic.

en.L: We remember the fish that we ate in Egypt for nothing, the cucumbers and the melons and the leeks and the onions and the garlic.
en.B: We remember the fish we used to eat in Egypt at no cost, and the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions and the garlic.
en.R: We remember all the fish we ate in Egypt. It did not cost us anything! We also had cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic.

decisions.choice: for nothing: free, without paying
decisions.reason: The word means "without cost". The Nile gave plenty of fish (Exodus 7:18, 21; Isaiah 19:8), and the people remember it as food they did not have to pay for. They forget that in Egypt they were slaves whose labor was the price (Exodus 1:13-14).

decisions.choice: cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, garlic: the vegetables of the Nile valley
decisions.reason: These are the common foods of Egypt. Each word appears only here in the Bible, except "leeks", which is usually the word for grass or green plants. The plants meant are well known from Egypt, though the exact kinds cannot always be fixed: "melons" may be watermelons.

source.text: וְעַתָּ֛ה נַפְשֵׁ֥נוּ יְבֵשָׁ֖ה אֵ֣ין כֹּ֑ל בִּלְתִּ֖י אֶל־הַמָּ֥ן עֵינֵֽינוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And now our soul [is] dry; there is not anything except to the manna our eyes.

en.L: But now our soul [is] dried up; there is nothing at all except the manna before our eyes."
en.B: But now we are wasting away. There is nothing at all, and all we ever see is this manna!"
en.R: But now we have no strength left. There is nothing to eat. All we ever see is this manna!"

decisions.choice: our soul is dried up: we are withered, our strength is drained
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word often translated "soul" can mean the throat, the appetite or a person's life. "Dried up" pictures a plant withering. The people mean they are wasting away for lack of real food, though the phrase could also mean they have lost their appetite.

decisions.choice: nothing at all except the manna before our eyes
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is short and abrupt: "nothing at all, except to the manna our eyes". It means that the manna is all they ever see. Manna is the food God gave from heaven each morning (Exodus 16:14-15, 35).

decisions.choice: we are wasting away / we have no strength left
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the picture. Literal keeps "our soul is dried up".

source.text: וְהַמָּ֕ן כִּזְרַע־גַּ֖ד ה֑וּא וְעֵינ֖וֹ כְּעֵ֥ין הַבְּדֹֽלַח׃

records.literal_gloss: And the manna like seed of coriander [was] it, and its appearance like [the] appearance of the bdellium.

en.L: And the manna, it [was] like coriander seed, and its appearance [was] like the appearance of bdellium.
en.B: The manna was like coriander seed, and it looked like bdellium.
en.R: The manna was shaped like little coriander seeds. It was the color of a pale, clear gum called bdellium.

decisions.choice: coriander seed: a small, round, pale seed
decisions.reason: Coriander seeds are small and round. Exodus 16:31 gives the same comparison and adds that the manna was white and tasted like wafers made with honey.

decisions.choice: bdellium: a pale, translucent resin
decisions.reason: The word appears elsewhere only in Genesis 2:12, among the treasures of the land of Havilah. It is most likely a fragrant resin, yellowish and clear, though some take it to be a pearl or a precious stone. Either way, the manna had a pale, shining look.

decisions.choice: a pale, clear gum called bdellium
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the name and says what kind of thing it was, so that the comparison makes sense.

source.text: שָׁטוּ֩ הָעָ֨ם וְלָֽקְט֜וּ וְטָחֲנ֣וּ בָרֵחַ֗יִם א֤וֹ דָכוּ֙ בַּמְּדֹכָ֔ה וּבִשְּׁלוּ֙ בַּפָּר֔וּר וְעָשׂ֥וּ אֹת֖וֹ עֻג֑וֹת וְהָיָ֣ה טַעְמ֔וֹ כְּטַ֖עַם לְשַׁ֥ד הַשָּֽׁמֶן׃

records.literal_gloss: Went about the people and gathered and ground in the mill or pounded in the mortar, and boiled in the pot and made it cakes; and was its taste like [the] taste of cake of the oil.

en.L: The people went about and gathered [it] and ground [it] in the mill or pounded [it] in the mortar, and boiled [it] in the pot and made it [into] cakes; and its taste was like the taste of cakes [made with] oil.
en.B: The people went around gathering it. They ground it with millstones or crushed it in a mortar, then boiled it in a pot and made it into cakes. It tasted like pastry baked with olive oil.
en.R: The people walked around and picked it up. They ground it between stones or pounded it in a bowl. Then they cooked it in a pot and made flat loaves out of it. It tasted like bread made with olive oil.

decisions.choice: cake of oil: something rich, made with olive oil
decisions.reason: The word translated "cake" is rare; it appears elsewhere only in Psalm 32:4, where it means moisture or freshness. Here it seems to mean a rich food made with oil, so the manna had a rich, oily taste. Exodus 16:31 compares it to wafers with honey.

decisions.choice: mill, mortar: household tools for grinding grain
decisions.reason: The mill was a pair of stones, a lower one and an upper one rubbed over it by hand. A mortar was a bowl in which grain was crushed with a pestle. The people treated manna like grain.

decisions.choice: went about ... gathered: what the people did every day
decisions.reason: The verbs describe a regular practice, what the people did each morning when manna came (Exodus 16:21).

decisions.choice: gathered [it], ground [it] ...
decisions.reason: Hebrew can leave the object of these verbs unsaid, since it is clear that the manna is meant. Literal brackets "it"; Balanced says it once at the start of each sentence.

source.text: וּבְרֶ֧דֶת הַטַּ֛ל עַל־הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֖ה לָ֑יְלָה יֵרֵ֥ד הַמָּ֖ן עָלָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And when came down the dew on the camp [at] night, came down the manna on it.

en.L: And when the dew came down on the camp [at] night, the manna came down on it.
en.B: Whenever the dew settled on the camp at night, the manna came down with it.
en.R: At night, when the dew fell on the camp, the manna fell along with it.

decisions.choice: came down: every night, again and again
decisions.reason: The verb describes what happened regularly. The manna came with the dew each night, so it was there in the morning when the dew lifted (Exodus 16:13-14).

decisions.choice: on it: on the dew, or with it on the camp
decisions.reason: The word can mean "on it" or "with it". Exodus 16:13-14 shows the dew lying around the camp and the manna left on the ground when the dew lifted, so the manna lay with or on the dew.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁמַ֨ע מֹשֶׁ֜ה אֶת־הָעָ֗ם בֹּכֶה֙ לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָ֔יו אִ֖ישׁ לְפֶ֣תַח אָהֳל֑וֹ וַיִּֽחַר־אַ֤ף יְהוָה֙ מְאֹ֔ד וּבְעֵינֵ֥י מֹשֶׁ֖ה רָֽע׃

records.literal_gloss: And heard Moses the people weeping by its clans, each at [the] entrance of his tent; and burned [the] anger of Yahweh greatly, and in [the] eyes of Moses [it was] evil.

en.L: And Moses heard the people weeping by their clans, each at the entrance of his tent; and the anger of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} burned greatly, and in the eyes of Moses [it was] evil.
en.B: Moses heard the people weeping, family by family, everyone at the entrance of their tent. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} became very angry, and Moses was deeply troubled.
en.R: Moses heard the people crying in every family. Each person was standing in the doorway of their tent and crying. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} became very angry, and Moses was very upset too.

decisions.choice: by their clans, each at the entrance of his tent: the weeping went through the whole camp
decisions.reason: Israel camped by tribes and clans (2:34). The weeping was not a few voices but family after family, each at its own tent, out in the open where everyone could hear.

decisions.choice: in the eyes of Moses it was evil: Moses was displeased and distressed
decisions.reason: "Evil in someone's eyes" means that a person sees something as bad and is upset by it. It can mean that Moses was displeased with the people, or that the whole situation, their weeping and God's anger, distressed him. His prayer in verses 11-15 shows his distress.

decisions.choice: everyone at the entrance of their tent
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "each" (literally "a man") here means each person, as the whole people was weeping. Balanced and Readable use "everyone" and "each person", which take no gender setting; Literal keeps "each ... his".

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר מֹשֶׁ֜ה אֶל־יְהוָ֗ה לָמָ֤ה הֲרֵעֹ֨תָ֙ לְעַבְדֶּ֔ךָ וְלָ֛מָּה לֹא־מָצָ֥תִי חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינֶ֑יךָ לָשׂ֗וּם אֶת־מַשָּׂ֛א כָּל־הָעָ֥ם הַזֶּ֖ה עָלָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Moses to Yahweh, why have you done evil to your slave? And why not have I found favor in your eyes, to put [the] burden of all the people the this on me?

en.L: And Moses said to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "Why have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} done evil to {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} slave? And why have I not found favor in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} eyes, that [you] put the burden of all this people on me?
en.B: Moses said to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "Why have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} brought this trouble on {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} servant? Why do I find no favor with {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} load me with the burden of this whole people?
en.R: Moses said to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "Why have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} made things so hard for me, {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} servant? Why are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} not pleased with me? You have made me responsible for all these people, and it is too heavy a load!

decisions.choice: done evil to: brought harm or trouble on
decisions.reason: The verb is from the same root as "evil" in verses 1 and 10. Moses does not accuse God of wrongdoing in a moral sense; he asks why God has brought this trouble on him.

decisions.choice: your slave: Moses speaking of himself as one who belongs to God
decisions.reason: Moses calls himself God's slave, a humble way of speaking to a superior. God himself calls Moses "my servant" (12:7-8). The word is the one used for a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired worker.

decisions.choice: the burden of all this people: the weight of leading and caring for them
decisions.reason: The word means a load carried on the back. Moses uses it of the whole people, whom he must care for alone. The same word returns in verse 17, where God promises others to share it (compare Deuteronomy 1:9-12).

decisions.choice: your servant
decisions.reason: As the style guide sets out, the word is "slave" at Literal and "servant" at Balanced and Readable. Here it is a title of humility, not a point about slavery.

decisions.choice: three short sentences
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the second question in two: the plain complaint, then the reason for it.

source.text: הֶאָנֹכִ֣י הָרִ֗יתִי אֵ֚ת כָּל־הָעָ֣ם הַזֶּ֔ה אִם־אָנֹכִ֖י יְלִדְתִּ֑יהוּ כִּֽי־תֹאמַ֨ר אֵלַ֜י שָׂאֵ֣הוּ בְחֵיקֶ֗ךָ כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר יִשָּׂ֤א הָאֹמֵן֙ אֶת־הַיֹּנֵ֔ק עַ֚ל הָֽאֲדָמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִשְׁבַּ֖עְתָּ לַאֲבֹתָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: [Is it] I [who] conceived all the people the this, or I [who] gave birth to it, that you say to me, carry it in your bosom, just as carries the nurse the sucking child, to the land which you swore to its fathers?

en.L: Was it I [who] conceived all this people? Or was it I [who] gave birth to it, that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} say to me, 'Carry it in your bosom, as the nurse carries the nursing child,' to the land that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} swore to its fathers?
en.B: Was it I who conceived this whole people? Was it I who gave birth to them, so that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} tell me, 'Hold them close and carry them, as a guardian carries a nursing baby,' all the way to the land {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} promised on oath to their ancestors?
en.R: Am I the mother of all these people? Did I give birth to them? Then why do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} tell me to carry them in my arms like a baby, all the way to the land {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} promised to their ancestors?

decisions.choice: was it I?: Moses stresses himself, implying God is the true parent
decisions.reason: In both questions the pronoun "I" is written out although the verb already shows the subject, which stresses it: "was it I?" The questions expect the answer no. Elsewhere God calls Israel his firstborn son (Exodus 4:22) and is pictured as Israel's father who carried him (Deuteronomy 1:31; 32:18), so the point is that Israel is God's child, not Moses'.

decisions.choice: the nurse: one who looks after and carries a small child
decisions.reason: The word is a masculine form, used of guardians who raise children (2 Kings 10:1, 5; Isaiah 49:23). Moses pictures himself having to carry the whole people like a helpless infant at the breast.

decisions.choice: the land that you swore to its fathers: Moses' words, not God's
decisions.reason: "You swore" refers to God, so these are Moses' words added to the command he quotes. God promised the land on oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 26:3; Exodus 32:13).

decisions.choice: a guardian
decisions.reason: "Nurse" in modern English suggests a woman in a hospital. Balanced uses "guardian" for the man who carries and cares for a child; Literal keeps "nurse".

decisions.choice: Am I the mother ...? ... Then why ...
decisions.reason: Readable turns Moses' questions into short questions a young reader can follow, and gives God's command as reported speech. "Mother" makes plain what "conceive" and "give birth" mean here.

source.text: מֵאַ֤יִן לִי֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר לָתֵ֖ת לְכָל־הָעָ֣ם הַזֶּ֑ה כִּֽי־יִבְכּ֤וּ עָלַי֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר תְּנָה־לָּ֥נוּ בָשָׂ֖ר וְנֹאכֵֽלָה׃

records.literal_gloss: From where [is there] to me meat to give to all the people the this? For they weep to me, saying, give to us meat that we may eat.

en.L: From where [is there] meat for me to give to all this people? For they weep to me, saying, 'Give us meat, that we may eat.'
en.B: Where could I find meat for this whole people? They keep crying to me, 'Give us meat to eat!'
en.R: Where can I get meat for all these people? They keep crying and saying to me, 'Give us meat to eat!'

decisions.choice: they weep to me: they keep on weeping
decisions.reason: The verb form describes what is going on and keeps happening. The weeping of verses 4 and 10 is still going on as Moses speaks.

decisions.choice: keep crying
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "keep" to show the ongoing weeping; Literal keeps the plain verb.

source.text: לֹֽא־אוּכַ֤ל אָנֹכִי֙ לְבַדִּ֔י לָשֵׂ֖את אֶת־כָּל־הָעָ֣ם הַזֶּ֑ה כִּ֥י כָבֵ֖ד מִמֶּֽנִּי׃

records.literal_gloss: Not am able I by myself to carry all the people the this, for [it is] heavy for me.

en.L: I am not able, I by myself, to carry all this people, for [it is too] heavy for me.
en.B: I cannot carry this whole people on my own. The load is too heavy for me.
en.R: I cannot take care of all these people by myself. It is too much for me.

decisions.choice: heavy: too great a weight to bear
decisions.reason: "Heavy" carries on the picture of the burden (verse 11) and of carrying a child (verse 12). Jethro had warned Moses of the same thing: the task is too heavy for you alone (Exodus 18:18).

decisions.choice: take care of ... too much for me
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the picture: carrying the people means caring for and leading them.

source.text: וְאִם־כָּ֣כָה׀אַתְּ־עֹ֣שֶׂה לִּ֗י הָרְגֵ֤נִי נָא֙ הָרֹ֔ג אִם־מָצָ֥אתִי חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינֶ֑יךָ וְאַל־אֶרְאֶ֖ה בְּרָעָתִֽי׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And if thus you [are] doing to me, kill me, please, killing, if I have found favor in your eyes; and let me not see my evil.

en.L: And if this is how {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are doing to me, kill me, please, outright, if I have found favor in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} eyes, and let me not see my misery."
en.B: If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are going to deal with me like this, then put me to death at once, if I have found favor with {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, and spare me from seeing my own ruin."
en.R: If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are going to keep treating me like this, please just let me die right now. If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} care for me at all, do not make me go through this misery any longer."

decisions.choice: you (feminine form): an unusual form of the word
decisions.reason: The pronoun "you" is written in a form that usually belongs to a woman. It is read as the ordinary "you", and the verb beside it is the ordinary masculine form. The same short spelling occurs in Deuteronomy 5:27 and Ezekiel 28:14. It does not change the meaning.

decisions.choice: kill me, please, killing: kill me outright
decisions.reason: A verb repeated with its own infinitive stresses it: "kill me at once", "just kill me". Elijah (1 Kings 19:4) and Jonah (Jonah 4:3) make similar requests in despair.

decisions.choice: my evil (my misery): the text as it stands
decisions.reason: An old Jewish scribal tradition lists this verse among a small number of places where scribes are said to have changed a word out of reverence for God. It says the original was "your evil", meaning the trouble God brings, and that "my" was written to avoid saying that of God. No known Hebrew manuscript has that reading. The text as written means Moses asks not to see his own ruin.

decisions.choice: If you care for me at all
decisions.reason: "If I have found favor in your eyes" is a polite way of asking. Readable gives the sense in plain words.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֜ה אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֗ה אֶסְפָה־לִּ֞י שִׁבְעִ֣ים אִישׁ֮ מִזִּקְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵל֒ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָדַ֔עְתָּ כִּי־הֵ֛ם זִקְנֵ֥י הָעָ֖ם וְשֹׁטְרָ֑יו וְלָקַחְתָּ֤ אֹתָם֙ אֶל־אֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֔ד וְהִֽתְיַצְּב֥וּ שָׁ֖ם עִמָּֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Yahweh to Moses, gather for me seventy man from [the] elders of Israel whom you know that they [are the] elders of the people and its officers, and take them to [the] tent of meeting, and let them station themselves there with you.

en.L: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Gather for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} seventy men from the elders of Israel whom you know to be the elders of the people and its officers, and take them to the tent of meeting, and let them station themselves there with you.
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Bring together for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} seventy of Israel's elders, men you know to be elders and officers among the people. Bring them to the tent of meeting and have them take their stand there with you.
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Choose seventy of Israel's elders for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. Choose men you know are respected elders and officials of the people. Bring them to the meeting tent, and have them stand there with you.

decisions.choice: elders: the senior men who led families and tribes
decisions.reason: Elders were the older heads of families and clans who spoke and decided for the people (Exodus 3:16; 24:1). Seventy elders had gone up the mountain with Moses and seen God (Exodus 24:9-11).

decisions.choice: its officers: officials who kept order and records
decisions.reason: The word is used for the Israelite foremen in Egypt (Exodus 5:6, 14) and later for officials who served beside judges (Deuteronomy 16:18). The seventy are to be men whom Moses already knows as leaders.

decisions.choice: station themselves: take their place and stand ready
decisions.reason: The verb means to take one's stand, often before God or a superior (Exodus 19:17). The elders are to stand with Moses in God's presence.

decisions.choice: officials
decisions.reason: Readable uses the more common word "officials" for the officers.

source.text: וְיָרַדְתִּ֗י וְדִבַּרְתִּ֣י עִמְּךָ֮ שָׁם֒ וְאָצַלְתִּ֗י מִן־הָר֛וּחַ אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָלֶ֖יךָ וְשַׂמְתִּ֣י עֲלֵיהֶ֑ם וְנָשְׂא֤וּ אִתְּךָ֙ בְּמַשָּׂ֣א הָעָ֔ם וְלֹא־תִשָּׂ֥א אַתָּ֖ה לְבַדֶּֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And I will come down and I will speak with you there, and I will take away from the spirit which [is] on you and I will put on them; and they will carry with you in [the] burden of the people, and not will carry you, you by yourself.

en.L: And I will come down and speak with you there, and I will take away some of the Spirit that [is] on you and put [it] on them; and they will carry the burden of the people with you, and you will not carry [it], you by yourself.
en.B: I will come down and speak with you there. I will take some of the Spirit that rests on you and place it on them. Then they will share the burden of the people with you, so that you will not have to carry it alone.
en.R: I will come down and talk with you there. I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put the Spirit on them too. Then they will help you take care of the people, and you will not have to do it all by yourself.

decisions.choice: the Spirit that is on you: God's Spirit, given to Moses for his task
decisions.reason: The spirit on Moses is not his own human spirit but God's, as Moses says in verse 29: "that Yahweh would put his Spirit on them". God gives it to equip people for a task, as with Bezalel (Exodus 31:3) and later Joshua (27:18). Taking some of it does not leave Moses with less; it means the same Spirit now rests on the seventy as well.

decisions.choice: take away: set apart and take some from
decisions.reason: The verb means to withdraw or set aside part of something. It is used only rarely and returns in verse 25, where God does what he says here.

decisions.choice: carry the burden ... not carry it alone: God answers Moses' complaint
decisions.reason: God takes up Moses' own words from verses 11 and 14. The help Jethro once advised (Exodus 18:22) is now given by God himself.

decisions.choice: Spirit, with a capital S
decisions.reason: Because verse 29 calls it Yahweh's Spirit, every level writes "Spirit" with a capital, as for "the Spirit of the LORD" elsewhere.

source.text: וְאֶל־הָעָ֨ם תֹּאמַ֜ר הִתְקַדְּשׁ֣וּ לְמָחָר֮ וַאֲכַלְתֶּ֣ם בָּשָׂר֒ כִּ֡י בְּכִיתֶם֩ בְּאָזְנֵ֨י יְהוָ֜ה לֵאמֹ֗ר מִ֤י יַאֲכִלֵ֨נוּ֙ בָּשָׂ֔ר כִּי־ט֥וֹב לָ֖נוּ בְּמִצְרָ֑יִם וְנָתַ֨ן יְהוָ֥ה לָכֶ֛ם בָּשָׂ֖ר וַאֲכַלְתֶּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And to the people you will say, consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you will eat meat; for you have wept in [the] ears of Yahweh, saying, who will feed us meat? For [it was] good for us in Egypt. And will give Yahweh to you meat, and you will eat.

en.L: And to the people you will say, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you will eat meat; for you have wept in the ears of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, saying, "Who will feed us meat? For [it was] good for us in Egypt." And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will give you meat, and you will eat.
en.B: And tell the people, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you will eat meat. You have wailed in the hearing of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "If only we had meat to eat! We were better off in Egypt!" So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will give you meat, and you will eat it.
en.R: Tell the people, 'Make yourselves holy and get ready for tomorrow, because you will eat meat. You cried where {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} could hear you. You said, "We wish we had meat to eat! Life was better for us in Egypt!" So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will give you meat, and you will eat it.

decisions.choice: consecrate yourselves: make yourselves ready to meet God
decisions.reason: To consecrate oneself meant to wash and set oneself apart before an event in which God would act (Exodus 19:10, 14-15; Joshua 3:5). Here it has a sharp edge: the people are to prepare for a meal that will bring judgment (verse 33).

decisions.choice: who will feed us meat?: God repeats the people's own words
decisions.reason: God quotes the people's cry from verse 4 and adds their claim that life was better in Egypt (compare Exodus 16:3). What they wished for, they will receive.

decisions.choice: make yourselves holy and get ready
decisions.reason: Readable gives both sides of the word: being set apart for God, and preparing.

source.text: לֹ֣א י֥וֹם אֶחָ֛ד תֹּאכְל֖וּן וְלֹ֣א יוֹמָ֑יִם וְלֹ֣א׀חֲמִשָּׁ֣ה יָמִ֗ים וְלֹא֙ עֲשָׂרָ֣ה יָמִ֔ים וְלֹ֖א עֶשְׂרִ֥ים יֽוֹם׃

records.literal_gloss: Not one day you will eat, and not two days, and not five days, and not ten days, and not twenty days,

en.L: Not one day will you eat, and not two days, and not five days, and not ten days, and not twenty days,
en.B: You will eat it not for one day, or two days, or five, or ten, or twenty days,
en.R: You will not eat it for just one day, or two days, or five days, or ten days, or even twenty days.

decisions.choice: not one day ... not twenty days: a rising list
decisions.reason: The list climbs step by step to build up to the answer in verse 20: a whole month. The sentence runs on into the next verse.

decisions.choice: a full stop at the end of the verse
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced end with a comma, since the sentence continues. Readable ends the sentence here and starts a new one in verse 20.

source.text: עַ֣ד׀חֹ֣דֶשׁ יָמִ֗ים עַ֤ד אֲשֶׁר־יֵצֵא֙ מֵֽאַפְּכֶ֔ם וְהָיָ֥ה לָכֶ֖ם לְזָרָ֑א יַ֗עַן כִּֽי־מְאַסְתֶּ֤ם אֶת־יְהוָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּקִרְבְּכֶ֔ם וַתִּבְכּ֤וּ לְפָנָיו֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר לָ֥מָּה זֶּ֖ה יָצָ֥אנוּ מִמִּצְרָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: until a month of days, until that it comes out from your nose and it becomes to you a loathsome thing, because that you have rejected Yahweh who [is] in your midst, and you have wept before him, saying, why [is] this [that] we came out from Egypt?

en.L: until a month of days, until it comes out of your nose and becomes loathsome to you, because you have rejected {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} who [is] in your midst, and have wept before {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saying, "Why [is] this [that] we came out of Egypt?"'"
en.B: but for a full month, until it pours out of your noses and turns your stomachs. For you have rejected {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, who is among you, and you have wailed before {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Why did we ever leave Egypt?"'"
en.R: You will eat it for a whole month, until you are so sick of it that it comes out of your nose! This will happen because you have turned away from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, who is right here with you. You cried to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and asked why you ever left Egypt.'"

decisions.choice: until it comes out of your nose and becomes loathsome: until you are sick of it
decisions.reason: The picture is of eating so much that it comes back up. The rare word "loathsome" means something that disgusts. The meat they crave will become something they cannot stand.

decisions.choice: you have rejected Yahweh who is among you
decisions.reason: God names what the weeping means. To long for Egypt is to reject the God who brought them out and who lives among them in the tabernacle (5:3; Exodus 29:45). The same verb for rejecting appears in 14:31.

decisions.choice: a month of days: a full month
decisions.reason: "A month of days" means a whole month, the full count of its days, as in Genesis 29:14.

decisions.choice: asked why you ever left Egypt
decisions.reason: Readable gives the people's question as reported speech, so that the quotation within a quotation within God's speech is easier to follow.

source.text: וַיֹּאמֶר֮ מֹשֶׁה֒ שֵׁשׁ־מֵא֥וֹת אֶ֨לֶף֙ רַגְלִ֔י הָעָ֕ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י בְּקִרְבּ֑וֹ וְאַתָּ֣ה אָמַ֗רְתָּ בָּשָׂר֙ אֶתֵּ֣ן לָהֶ֔ם וְאָכְל֖וּ חֹ֥דֶשׁ יָמִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Moses, six hundred thousand on foot [are] the people which I [am] in its midst, and you, you have said, meat I will give to them, and they will eat a month of days.

en.L: And Moses said, "600,000 on foot [are] the people in whose midst I [am], and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have said, 'Meat I will give to them, and they will eat a month of days.'
en.B: But Moses said, "I am among a people of 600,000 men on foot, and yet {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} say, 'I will give them meat, and they will eat it for a whole month!'
en.R: But Moses said, "There are 600,000 men here with me, besides the rest of the people. And {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} say, 'I will give them meat to eat for a whole month!'

decisions.choice: on foot: men who march on foot, the fighting men
decisions.reason: The word means foot soldiers or men on foot. The number matches the 600,000 men on foot who left Egypt, besides children (Exodus 12:37), and is a round figure for the census total of 603,550 (1:46). On the size of numbers given in "thousands", see the decision on the census in chapter 1.

decisions.choice: and you, you have said: Moses sets God's promise against the size of the people
decisions.reason: Moses writes out "you" to stress it. He is not refusing to believe, but he cannot see how the promise can be kept for so many.

decisions.choice: besides the rest of the people
decisions.reason: The number counts only the men (Exodus 12:37). Readable adds that the rest of the people are more besides, so that a young reader does not take 600,000 as the whole people.

source.text: הֲצֹ֧אן וּבָקָ֛ר יִשָּׁחֵ֥ט לָהֶ֖ם וּמָצָ֣א לָהֶ֑ם אִ֣ם אֶֽת־כָּל־דְּגֵ֥י הַיָּ֛ם יֵאָסֵ֥ף לָהֶ֖ם וּמָצָ֥א לָהֶֽם׃פ

records.literal_gloss: Flock and herd, will they be slaughtered for them, and will one find for them? Or all [the] fish of the sea will be gathered for them, and will one find for them?

en.L: Will flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, and will it be enough for them? Or will all the fish of the sea be gathered for them, and will it be enough for them?"
en.B: If flocks and herds were slaughtered for them, would they have enough? If all the fish in the sea were caught for them, would they have enough?"
en.R: Even if we killed all our sheep and cattle, would that be enough for them? Even if we caught all the fish in the sea, would that be enough?"

decisions.choice: will one find for them: will it be enough for them
decisions.reason: "Find for them" means "suffice for them", "be enough". Moses' questions expect the answer no: not even all the animals or all the fish would be enough for so many.

decisions.choice: flock and herd: sheep and goats, and cattle
decisions.reason: "Flock" means sheep and goats; "herd" means cattle. Israel had brought large flocks and herds from Egypt (Exodus 12:38), but to slaughter them would destroy the people's wealth.

decisions.choice: all our sheep and cattle
decisions.reason: Readable names the animals and adds "all" to make plain the size of what Moses imagines; the Hebrew uses "all" for the fish.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֶל־מֹשֶׁ֔ה הֲיַ֥ד יְהוָ֖ה תִּקְצָ֑ר עַתָּ֥ה תִרְאֶ֛ה הֲיִקְרְךָ֥ דְבָרִ֖י אִם־לֹֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Yahweh to Moses, [is the] hand of Yahweh short? Now you will see whether will happen to you my word or not.

en.L: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Is the hand of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} short? Now you will see whether {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} word will happen for you or not."
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to Moses, "Is the reach of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} too short? Now you will see whether {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} word comes about for you or not."
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} answered Moses, "Do you think {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is not strong enough? Now you will see whether I do what I said or not."

decisions.choice: is the hand of Yahweh short?: is Yahweh's power limited?
decisions.reason: The hand stands for power. A short hand cannot reach far enough to save or to give (Isaiah 50:2; 59:1). God speaks of himself by his name, as if to say: do you think Yahweh cannot do this?

decisions.choice: whether my word will happen for you: whether what I have said will come true
decisions.reason: "My word" is God's promise of meat in verses 18-20. Moses will see it fulfilled with his own eyes (verse 31).

decisions.choice: the reach of the LORD
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture of a hand that cannot reach far enough, in a form English can follow. Literal keeps "hand ... short"; Readable gives the sense.

source.text: וַיֵּצֵ֣א מֹשֶׁ֗ה וַיְדַבֵּר֙ אֶל־הָעָ֔ם אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וַיֶּאֱסֹ֞ף שִׁבְעִ֥ים אִישׁ֙ מִזִּקְנֵ֣י הָעָ֔ם וַֽיַּעֲמֵ֥ד אֹתָ֖ם סְבִיבֹ֥ת הָאֹֽהֶל׃

records.literal_gloss: And went out Moses and spoke to the people the words of Yahweh, and gathered seventy man from [the] elders of the people, and stationed them around the tent.

en.L: And Moses went out and spoke to the people the words of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and he gathered seventy men from the elders of the people and stationed them around the tent.
en.B: So Moses went out and told the people what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had said. He gathered seventy men from the elders of the people and had them stand around the tent.
en.R: So Moses went out and told the people what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had said. Then he brought together seventy of the elders and had them stand around the meeting tent.

decisions.choice: the tent: the tent of meeting
decisions.reason: "The tent" is the tent of meeting named in verse 16. Moses goes out from it to the people and brings the elders back to stand around it. In Exodus 33:7 a tent of meeting stood outside the camp, and verses 26 and 30 also picture the elders going out of the camp to the tent and coming back.

decisions.choice: the meeting tent
decisions.reason: Readable names the tent, so the reader knows which tent is meant.

source.text: וַיֵּ֨רֶד יְהוָ֥ה׀בֶּעָנָן֮ וַיְדַבֵּ֣ר אֵלָיו֒ וַיָּ֗אצֶל מִן־הָר֨וּחַ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָלָ֔יו וַיִּתֵּ֕ן עַל־שִׁבְעִ֥ים אִ֖ישׁ הַזְּקֵנִ֑ים וַיְהִ֗י כְּנ֤וֹחַ עֲלֵיהֶם֙ הָר֔וּחַ וַיִּֽתְנַבְּא֖וּ וְלֹ֥א יָסָֽפוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And came down Yahweh in the cloud and spoke to him, and took away from the spirit which [was] on him and put on seventy man the elders; and it was, when rested on them the spirit, and they prophesied, and not they did again.

en.L: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came down in the cloud and spoke to him, and took away some of the Spirit that [was] on him and put [it] on the seventy men, the elders; and it happened, when the Spirit rested on them, that they prophesied, but they did not do [it] again.
en.B: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came down in the cloud and spoke to him. He took some of the Spirit that was on Moses and put it on the seventy elders. As soon as the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did not do so again.
en.R: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came down in the cloud and spoke to Moses. He took some of the Spirit that was on Moses and put the Spirit on the seventy elders. When the Spirit came on them, they began to speak like prophets. But they did this only that one time.

decisions.choice: they prophesied: they spoke and acted as prophets, moved by the Spirit
decisions.reason: The verb form here describes behaving as a prophet. It does not say that they spoke a message about the future. As with Saul in 1 Samuel 10:5-13 and 19:20-24, it was an outward sign, seen and heard by others, that God's Spirit had come on them.

decisions.choice: they did not do it again: it happened this one time
decisions.reason: The verb means "add, do again". The prophesying was a sign, given once, that God had put his Spirit on the seventy. Some early translations read the same letters as a verb meaning "stop", giving "and they did not stop". The Hebrew as written reads "they did not do it again".

decisions.choice: Yahweh came down in the cloud
decisions.reason: God does what he promised in verse 17. The cloud marked his presence over the tent (9:15-16; 12:5; Exodus 33:9).

decisions.choice: Moses for "him"
decisions.reason: In Hebrew "him" can only be Moses here. Balanced and Readable write the name, since in English "him" might seem to mean God.

source.text: וַיִּשָּׁאֲר֣וּ שְׁנֵֽי־אֲנָשִׁ֣ים׀בַּֽמַּחֲנֶ֡ה שֵׁ֣ם הָאֶחָ֣ד׀אֶלְדָּ֡ד וְשֵׁם֩ הַשֵּׁנִ֨י מֵידָ֜ד וַתָּ֧נַח עֲלֵיהֶ֣ם הָר֗וּחַ וְהֵ֨מָּה֙ בַּכְּתֻבִ֔ים וְלֹ֥א יָצְא֖וּ הָאֹ֑הֱלָה וַיִּֽתְנַבְּא֖וּ בַּֽמַּחֲנֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And remained two men in the camp; [the] name of the one Eldad, and [the] name of the second Medad, and rested on them the spirit; and they [were] among the written, and not they had gone out to the tent; and they prophesied in the camp.

en.L: And two men had remained in the camp; the name of the one [was] Eldad, and the name of the second Medad, and the Spirit rested on them; and they [were] among those written, but they had not gone out to the tent; and they prophesied in the camp.
en.B: Two men, however, had stayed behind in the camp, one named Eldad and the other Medad. The Spirit rested on them too. They were among those listed, but they had not gone out to the tent, and they prophesied in the camp.
en.R: But two men named Eldad and Medad had stayed in the camp. Their names were on the list of elders, but they had not gone out to the tent. The Spirit came on them too, and they began to speak like prophets right there in the camp.

decisions.choice: among those written: on the list of the seventy
decisions.reason: "Written" means their names had been recorded. They were among the elders chosen in verse 16, though the text does not say why they did not go out to the tent.

decisions.choice: the Spirit rested on them in the camp
decisions.reason: The Spirit came on these two away from the tent and away from Moses. God's gift is not bound to the place where Moses stood, which is the point of Moses' answer in verse 29.

decisions.choice: the list first, then the Spirit
decisions.reason: Readable explains first who the two men were, then tells what happened, so that the story is easier to follow.

source.text: וַיָּ֣רָץ הַנַּ֔עַר וַיַּגֵּ֥ד לְמֹשֶׁ֖ה וַיֹּאמַ֑ר אֶלְדָּ֣ד וּמֵידָ֔ד מִֽתְנַבְּאִ֖ים בַּֽמַּחֲנֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And ran the young man and told Moses and said, Eldad and Medad [are] prophesying in the camp.

en.L: And the young man ran and told Moses, and said, "Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp."
en.B: A young man ran and told Moses, "Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp!"
en.R: A young man ran to tell Moses. He said, "Eldad and Medad are speaking like prophets in the camp!"

decisions.choice: the young man: a certain young man, not named
decisions.reason: The article points to one particular young man in the story, but he is not named. Hebrew often uses the article this way for a person who has a part in the scene.

decisions.choice: a young man
decisions.reason: English introduces an unnamed person with "a". Literal keeps "the".

source.text: וַיַּ֜עַן יְהוֹשֻׁ֣עַ בִּן־נ֗וּן מְשָׁרֵ֥ת מֹשֶׁ֛ה מִבְּחֻרָ֖יו וַיֹּאמַ֑ר אֲדֹנִ֥י מֹשֶׁ֖ה כְּלָאֵֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered Joshua son of Nun, [the] attendant of Moses from his youth, and said, my lord Moses, restrain them.

en.L: And Joshua son of Nun, the attendant of Moses from his youth, answered and said, "My lord Moses, restrain them!"
en.B: Joshua son of Nun, who had served as Moses' assistant since he was young, spoke up: "My lord Moses, stop them!"
en.R: Joshua son of Nun had been Moses' helper since he was a young man. He said, "Moses, sir, make them stop!"

decisions.choice: from his youth: since he was young, or one of his chosen men
decisions.reason: The word can come from a noun meaning "youth", giving "from his youth", or from one meaning "chosen men", giving "one of his chosen men". Both fit: Joshua was a young man in Moses' service (Exodus 33:11) and had been chosen for tasks such as leading the battle against Amalek (Exodus 17:9).

decisions.choice: attendant: a personal assistant, not a slave
decisions.reason: The word is not the word for a slave. It means one who waits on and helps a leader, and it is used of Joshua in Exodus 24:13 and 33:11 and of Elisha with Elijah (1 Kings 19:21).

decisions.choice: restrain them: hold them back, make them stop
decisions.reason: The verb means to hold back or shut in. Joshua wants Moses to stop the two men, perhaps because they prophesy outside the tent and apart from Moses.

decisions.choice: Moses, sir
decisions.reason: "My lord" is a polite way to speak to a superior. Readable uses "sir", which young readers know as a respectful address.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ מֹשֶׁ֔ה הַֽמְקַנֵּ֥א אַתָּ֖ה לִ֑י וּמִ֨י יִתֵּ֜ן כָּל־עַ֤ם יְהוָה֙ נְבִיאִ֔ים כִּי־יִתֵּ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־רוּח֖וֹ עֲלֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to him Moses, jealous [are] you for me? And who will give all [the] people of Yahweh [were] prophets, that would put Yahweh his spirit on them!

en.L: And Moses said to him, "Are you jealous for me? And who will give [that] all the people of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [were] prophets, that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} would put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Spirit on them!"
en.B: But Moses said to him, "Are you being jealous on my behalf? If only {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} would put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Spirit on all {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people and make every one of them a prophet!"
en.R: But Moses said to him, "Are you upset because you are trying to protect my honor? I wish {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} would put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Spirit on all of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people, so that every one of them could be a prophet!"

decisions.choice: jealous for me: zealous to guard my position
decisions.reason: The verb means burning zeal for someone's rights or honor. Joshua is zealous for Moses' standing as the one through whom God speaks. Moses does not want that kind of protection.

decisions.choice: who will give ...: if only, a strong wish
decisions.reason: "Who will give?" is a Hebrew way of expressing a wish (compare verse 4 and Deuteronomy 5:29). Moses wishes that the gift given to the seventy were given to all God's people. Joel 2:28-29 later promises that God will pour out his Spirit on all.

decisions.choice: the LORD would put his Spirit on all his people and make every one of them a prophet
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the two halves of the wish into one sentence with God as its subject, which reads more naturally. The meaning is the same: all the people prophets, through God's Spirit on them.

source.text: וַיֵּאָסֵ֥ף מֹשֶׁ֖ה אֶל־הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֑ה ה֖וּא וְזִקְנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And withdrew Moses to the camp, he and [the] elders of Israel.

en.L: And Moses withdrew to the camp, he and the elders of Israel.
en.B: Then Moses and the elders of Israel went back to the camp.
en.R: Then Moses and the elders of Israel went back to the camp.

decisions.choice: withdrew: gathered himself back, returned
decisions.reason: The verb usually means "be gathered". With "to the camp" it means that Moses went back into the camp from the tent, which stood outside it (Exodus 33:7).

decisions.choice: went back
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the plain verb for returning.

source.text: וְר֜וּחַ נָסַ֣ע׀מֵאֵ֣ת יְהוָ֗ה וַיָּ֣גָז שַׂלְוִים֮ מִן־הַיָּם֒ וַיִּטֹּ֨שׁ עַל־הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֜ה כְּדֶ֧רֶךְ י֣וֹם כֹּ֗ה וּכְדֶ֤רֶךְ יוֹם֙ כֹּ֔ה סְבִיב֖וֹת הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֑ה וּכְאַמָּתַ֖יִם עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָאָֽרֶץ׃

records.literal_gloss: And a wind set out from with Yahweh and drove quails from the sea and let fall by the camp, about a way of a day thus and about a way of a day thus, around the camp, and about two cubits on [the] face of the land.

en.L: And a wind went out from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and it drove quail from the sea and let [them] fall beside the camp, about a day's journey this way and about a day's journey that way, around the camp, and about two cubits above the face of the ground.
en.B: Then a wind went out from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. It swept quail in from the sea and brought them down beside the camp, for about a day's walk in one direction and a day's walk in the other, all around the camp, about {{units:3 feet|two cubits}} above the ground.
en.R: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent a wind. It blew in quail from the sea and brought them down around the camp. They covered the ground as far as a person could walk in a day in every direction. They were about {{units:3 feet|two cubits}} above the ground.

decisions.choice: wind: the same word as "spirit"
decisions.reason: The word that means "spirit" in verses 17-29 here means "wind". The God who gave his Spirit to the elders now sends his wind to bring the meat, both coming from him.

decisions.choice: quail: small birds that migrate across the sea
decisions.reason: Quail cross the Mediterranean Sea and the Gulf of Suez in spring and autumn, and tired flocks come down to the ground in great numbers. God fed Israel quail before, in the wilderness of Sin (Exodus 16:13; Psalm 78:26-28).

decisions.choice: about two cubits above the ground: the quail lay piled up, or flew low
alternatives: flying about two cubits above the ground
decisions.reason: The phrase may mean the quail lay heaped on the ground to a depth of about two cubits, or that they flew about two cubits above the ground, low enough to be caught by hand. Both readings have long been held; verse 32, where the people gather them for two days, fits either.

decisions.choice: about 3 feet, with two cubits as the alternative
decisions.reason: A cubit is about 18 inches, so two cubits are about 3 feet. Literal keeps "two cubits".

decisions.choice: as far as a person could walk in a day in every direction
decisions.reason: Readable explains "a day's journey this way and a day's journey that way".

source.text: וַיָּ֣קָם הָעָ֡ם כָּל־הַיּוֹם֩ הַה֨וּא וְכָל־הַלַּ֜יְלָה וְכֹ֣ל׀י֣וֹם הַֽמָּחֳרָ֗ת וַיַּֽאַסְפוּ֙ אֶת־הַשְּׂלָ֔ו הַמַּמְעִ֕יט אָסַ֖ף עֲשָׂרָ֣ה חֳמָרִ֑ים וַיִּשְׁטְח֤וּ לָהֶם֙ שָׁט֔וֹחַ סְבִיב֖וֹת הַֽמַּחֲנֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And rose the people all the day the that and all the night and all [the] day of the next day, and gathered the quail; the [one] gathering least gathered ten homers; and spread out for themselves spreading around the camp.

en.L: And the people rose up all that day and all the night and all the next day and gathered the quail; the [one who] gathered least gathered ten homers; and they spread [them] out for themselves all around the camp.
en.B: The people were up all that day, all night and all the next day gathering the quail. The one who gathered least gathered {{units:about 60 bushels|ten homers}}. They spread them out for themselves all around the camp.
en.R: So the people stayed up all that day, all that night and all the next day, gathering quail. Even the person who gathered the least gathered {{units:about 60 bushels|ten homers}}. Then they spread the birds out all around the camp to dry them.

decisions.choice: ten homers: a huge amount
decisions.reason: A homer was the largest dry measure, about 6 bushels (the load of a donkey), so ten homers is about 60 bushels. Even the one who gathered least took far more than anyone could eat.

decisions.choice: spread out for themselves: laid out to dry
decisions.reason: Meat was dried in the sun to keep it, as fish was dried in Egypt. The people laid the birds out all around the camp to keep them for later.

decisions.choice: all that day and all the night and all the next day: without stopping
decisions.reason: The list of day, night and day shows the people gathering for some thirty-six hours on end, with the craving of verse 4 now out of control.

decisions.choice: to dry them
decisions.reason: Readable says why the birds were spread out, as the culture decision explains.

source.text: הַבָּשָׂ֗ר עוֹדֶ֨נּוּ֙ בֵּ֣ין שִׁנֵּיהֶ֔ם טֶ֖רֶם יִכָּרֵ֑ת וְאַ֤ף יְהוָה֙ חָרָ֣ה בָעָ֔ם וַיַּ֤ךְ יְהוָה֙ בָּעָ֔ם מַכָּ֖ה רַבָּ֥ה מְאֹֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: The meat still [was] between their teeth, not yet was it cut off, and [the] anger of Yahweh burned against the people, and struck Yahweh among the people a blow great very.

en.L: The meat [was] still between their teeth, not yet cut off, when the anger of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} burned against the people, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} struck the people with a very great plague.
en.B: While the meat was still between their teeth, before it had been chewed, the anger of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} flared up against the people, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} struck them with a terrible plague.
en.R: The people were still chewing the meat when {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} became angry with them. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} sent a terrible sickness among the people.

decisions.choice: not yet cut off: before it was chewed, or before it ran out
decisions.reason: The verb means "be cut off". It may mean that the meat was not yet chewed and swallowed, so that the judgment came at once, while they were eating. Or it may mean that the supply was not yet used up, so that the judgment came during the month of verse 20.

decisions.choice: a blow, very great: a deadly plague
decisions.reason: The word means a blow or stroke, often a plague sent by God (Deuteronomy 28:59). The text does not describe it, but verse 34 shows that many died. Psalm 78:30-31 looks back on this event.

decisions.choice: a terrible sickness
decisions.reason: Readable uses "sickness" for the plague, which young readers may not know as a word for a deadly disease.

source.text: וַיִּקְרָ֛א אֶת־שֵֽׁם־הַמָּק֥וֹם הַה֖וּא קִבְר֣וֹת הַֽתַּאֲוָ֑ה כִּי־שָׁם֙ קָֽבְר֔וּ אֶת־הָעָ֖ם הַמִּתְאַוִּֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And called [one] the name of the place the that Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people the craving.

en.L: And [one] called the name of that place Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who craved.
en.B: So that place was named Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had craved.
en.R: So that place was called Kibroth-hattaavah, which means "graves of craving." They gave it that name because they buried there the people who had wanted more food so badly.

decisions.choice: Kibroth-hattaavah: "graves of craving"
decisions.reason: The name joins the word for graves to the word for craving in verse 4. It names the place after what happened: those who craved meat were buried there. Israel's later memory of the wilderness recalls the place (33:16; Deuteronomy 9:22).

decisions.choice: the people who craved: those who had given in to the craving
decisions.reason: The verb is the same as in verse 4. The text does not say that every Israelite died, only those who had craved.

decisions.choice: which means "graves of craving"
decisions.reason: Readable explains the name, as it does for Taberah in verse 3.

source.text: מִקִּבְר֧וֹת הַֽתַּאֲוָ֛ה נָסְע֥וּ הָעָ֖ם חֲצֵר֑וֹת וַיִּהְי֖וּ בַּחֲצֵרֽוֹת׃פ

records.literal_gloss: From Kibroth-hattaavah set out the people [to] Hazeroth, and they were in Hazeroth.

en.L: From Kibroth-hattaavah the people set out [to] Hazeroth, and they were at Hazeroth.
en.B: From Kibroth-hattaavah the people moved on to Hazeroth, and they stayed at Hazeroth.
en.R: Then the people left Kibroth-hattaavah and traveled to Hazeroth, and they stayed there.

decisions.choice: Hazeroth: a camp on the way through the wilderness
decisions.reason: The name means "enclosures" or "settlements". It is the next camp in the list of 33:17, and the story of chapter 12 takes place there (12:16). Its site is not known for certain.

decisions.choice: [to] Hazeroth
decisions.reason: Hebrew can name the goal of a journey without a word for "to". Literal brackets it.
